title: WLAN Architecture: The Complete Beginner's Guide

scenes.narration: Managing one access point is easy. Managing five hundred is chaos. You need a central dispatcher.

scenes.heading: Pizza delivery
scenes.narration: A pizza shop starts with a few drivers, each with their own map and phone. Every driver makes their own decisions, and that's autonomous mode. As the city grows, drivers get lost and orders clash. So the shop opens a dispatch office, the wireless controller. Drivers still drive and carry the pizzas, but the office decides the routes and keeps everyone coordinated. Those drivers are lightweight access points, and they talk to the dispatcher using a tunnel called CAPWAP.

items.story: The phone line to the office

scenes.heading: Three models
scenes.narration: There are a few ways to arrange it. A central controller manages every access point from one place. FlexConnect lets remote offices switch traffic locally while still managed centrally. And cloud managed, like Meraki, needs no on site controller, but does need the internet.

rows.label: Where's the brain
rows.r: Cloud, or central with local switching

scenes.heading: Common mix-ups
scenes.narration: Three mix-ups. CAPWAP uses U D P, not T C P. Control uses port fifty-two forty-six, and data uses fifty-two forty-seven. Not all traffic must go through the controller, because FlexConnect can switch it locally. And autonomous access points are still used in small sites.

items.wrong: All traffic goes through the WLC

scenes.narration: So, to recap. Autonomous access points work alone, and lightweight ones need a controller. They talk to the controller using CAPWAP over U D P. FlexConnect keeps traffic local at remote sites. Ready to practise? Try the Courseiva WLAN architecture lab.
